attributes.title: Level 4

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use comments to create multiple sections in the editor to better organize your code?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What code might be placed underneath each comment?

❓ How do you create blank lines in the JavaScript editor?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡  Explain to the ninja that typing // tells the project to skip over the text that follows and move onto the next line of code. Just as when naming sprites, it’s useful to be short and descriptive when writing comments. 

💡  Encourage the ninja to use best practices when adding comments to their code. It’s helpful to space out comments in the editor, so that code can be placed in the lines between them. They can use the Enter key to create blank lines between comments. They should also add a space after the slashes in the comment, before adding the text.
steps.instructions:
Begin the project by adding code comments to organize where the code will go in the editor!


Add comments with these descriptions to the project: set up, present sprite code, on A button pressed.


Start each comment with // and create several blank lines between each comment.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you replace mySprite with the name of the present sprite in setPosition and sayText?
steps.instructions:
Add a present sprite to the project for the user to open!


Open Sprites and drag out [sprite (img) of kind (kind)] underneath // present sprite code Click the palette to open the paint editor, then click My Assets at the top of the screen to select the present image. 

Replace mySprite with a simple name using camelCase that describes what it is, such as presentSprite.


Set the sprite’s position by opening Sprites and dragging [set (mySprite) position to x y] underneath the code that creates the sprite. Update the sprite’s name and the x (0-160) and y (0-120) parameters so that the sprite appears near the middle of the screen.


Code the sprite to give instructions for the user by opening Sprites, then dragging [(this) say (:))] underneath the code that sets the sprite’s position. Update the sprite’s name, then replace the text parameter with a string that tells the user to open the present. Customize the other parameters for the sayText function, too. 


Click ▶ to see the present sprite invite the user to see what’s inside!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you put the  if/else conditional inside the curly brackets of the controller.A event?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why should the conditional be placed inside the curly brackets of the controller.A event?

❓ What condition might the project check when the A button is pressed?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Help the ninja identify the curly brackets { } of the controller.A event and notice how they act as the container for the loop’s code to run through. After, point out the curly brackets { } of the if/else conditional. Prompt the ninja to consider how the conditional’s curly brackets act as the “container” for the code, and reflect on how this appeared in blocks. 

💡 Remind the ninja that code inside of curly brackets { } is called a block statement. This code is indented to make it easier for coders to read.
steps.instructions:
Code something to happen when the user “opens” the present!


Open Controller and drag [run code on (button) button (event)] underneath // on A button pressed. Use the default property A and default event argument ControllerButtonEvent.Pressed. 


Add a conditional to the project by opening Logic, then dragging [if/else] inside the curly brackets { } of the controller.A event. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text: 

if (true) {...} else {...}

The if/else conditional acts as a block statement nested inside the curly brackets of the event. It is indented, and contains its own set of curly brackets { } to place code inside of.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you check the syntax to make sure each pair of curly brackets has an opening and closing set?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ When will the code inside the else if condition run? When will the code inside the else condition run?

❓ Did you double check your code to make sure the conditions are listed in the correct order? Does each symbol have a matching pair?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Point out to the ninja that whenever a parenthesis or curly bracket is typed, the matching symbol will automatically appear on the editor. This is helpful for ensuring that the correct symbols and syntax are used in the code.

💡 Encourage the ninja to double check their work: is there an error message that pops up? Are the conditions in the correct order? Are the symbols in the right places? As needed, encourage the ninja to toggle back to blocks to notice how the conditional block compares to JavaScript text.
steps.instructions:
Add a third condition for the project to check for whenever the A button is pressed!


Click to the right of the keyword else, type if () , then {


When a single parenthesis or curly bracket is typed, the editor will automatically add the matching symbol. 


While the cursor is inside the new pair of curly brackets, press Enter to add a blank line below } else if () {


Then, place the cursor on the line below and type else between the remaining curly brackets so it looks like: } else {

steps.hints: ❓ Did you replace true inside the parentheses of the if condition with Math.percentChance(percentage)?
steps.instructions:
Add an element of chance to the project to give the user a surprise gift!


Delete true inside the parentheses of the if condition. Then, open Math and drag [(percentage) % chance] inside the parentheses. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:

Math.percentChance(0)

The percentChance function takes 1 parameter: a number between 0-100 that represents the percentage chance that the condition will be true. Replace 0 with 50 to set a certain sprite to appear 50% of the time the A button is pressed.


Copy (Ctrl + C) the existing percentChance code: Math.percentChance(50). Click the space inside the parentheses of the else if condition and press Ctrl + V to paste the section of code.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you select a different image for each line of the setImage code?
steps.instructions:
Change the sprite’s image when a certain condition is true!


Open Sprites and drag [set (mySprite) image to (img)] inside the curly brackets { } of the if, else if, and else conditions. 


In each new line of code, update mySprite with the present sprite’s name, then click the palette to select a different sprite from the gallery for each condition.


Click ▶ then press the A button to watch different sprites appear!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you type a different string in the sayText code that matches each sprite image?
steps.instructions:
Code each present to share a unique message!


Open Sprites and drag [(this) say (:))] underneath the code that changes the sprite’s image in the if, else if, and else condition’s block statements. 


In each new line of code, update mySprite with the present sprite’s name, then replace the text parameter with a string that tells the user about the present. Customize the other parameters for the sayText function, too. 


Be sure to change the text parameter for all 3 conditions so that each sprite image shares a different message.


Click ▶ to see sprites share unique messages when they appear on screen!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you update a different effect in the startEffect code for each condition?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What is similar about how a sprite effect is coded in JavaScript, versus a screen effect? 

❓ What sprite effect might you use to match each sprite’s image and message? 


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Point out to the ninja that setting effects requires them to use the dot operator . to select possible effects from the code completion tool. Both the sprite and screen effects use this feature and also have an optional duration parameter, to set how long the effect lasts.
steps.instructions:
Start a sprite effect when the present is opened!


Open Sprites, then drag [(mySprite) start (effect) effect] underneath the code that changes the sprite’s image in the if, else if, and else condition’s block statements. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text: 

mySprite.startEffect(effects.spray)

The startEffect function takes two parameters: effect and duration. Update the sprite’s name in the code, then delete .spray and retype the dot operator . to select an effect that matches the sprite’s image from the code completion tool. Type a comma , after the effect name, then type a number argument (in milliseconds) to set how long the effect should last. 


Be sure to change the effect parameter for all 3 conditions so that each effect matches its image.


Click ▶ to see different presents start different effects on screen!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you add game.reset() inside the controller.A event, but outside of the conditional’s curly brackets?
steps.instructions:
Reset the project after the present appears on the screen!


Create a blank line between the end of the else condition } and the end of the controller.A event }) 


Open Loops and drag [pause (100) ms] onto the new blank line. Replace 100 with a number argument that pauses the project for a longer amount of time than the sayText duration. 


Open Game and drag [reset game] into the editor, underneath the pause code. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:

game.reset()

﻿Now, after the pause delay, the game will reset. 


Click ▶ to see the project reset after the present appears on the screen!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you type a number between 1-15 to set the color parameter in the parentheses in scene.setBackgroundColor(color)?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What background color might you use as a backdrop for the project?

❓ What directions might tell the user how to play the game?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that they can always click on the palette for one of the images in the code to open the editor. Once opened, they can hover their cursor over each individual color to find the corresponding value to use as a background color.

💡 Remind the ninja that strings need to be placed inside of quotation marks and that parameters need to be separated by a comma, otherwise the code will not be able to run correctly.
steps.instructions:
Finish the project by adding a background color and directions!


Open Scene, drag [set background color to (color)] into the editor underneath // set up. Click between the parentheses to set a color parameter using a number 1-15.


Open Game and drag [set dialog frame to (frame)] onto a blank line underneath the background color code. Click the palette to the left of the line of code to choose a dialog frame image from the Gallery. 


Then, open Game and drag [show long text (str) (layout)] onto a blank line underneath the code to set the frame. Update the string and layout parameters, so that the dialog box shares directions for the user to follow.


Click ▶ to see the completed Grab Bag project!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you switch back to the blocks editor? What looks similar and what looks different?
steps.instructions:
Test out the project. Does it work as expected?


Switch to the blocks editor to see what the JavaScript code looks like in blocks! Notice what is similar about the code, and what looks different: how do the nested block statements appear in blocks, versus in JavaScript?

subgroups.title: Grab Bag!
subgroups.introduction: Create a project in JavaScript that uses conditionals and nested block statements to randomize what present the user receives!

validationItems.text: Use 1 sprite with a custom name, set its position, and have it say a message.
Use a button press event that runs code when the A button is pressed. Place a conditional statement inside the event.
Use percent chance functions to change the contents of the present.
Use the setImage function to create three different images for the present.
Use the sayText function to have all 3 presents say a different message.
Use the startEffect function to give each present a different effect.
Use a pause function before resetting the game.
Change the background color, add a dialog frame, and use long text to provide directions for the user.

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 4 of Blue Belt! In this level, you’ll learn more about conditionals and nested block statements. Nested block statements are created when code inside of curly brackets is placed inside of another chunk of code in curly brackets, such as placing a conditional inside of a forever loop. Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 4:

badges.title: Curly Brackets All the Way Down
badges.description: Use nested block statements to place one block statement inside another in JavaScript.

badges.title: If at First You Don’t Succeed
badges.description: Use  “if” and “if / else” statements in JavaScript.

badges.title: ...or Else
badges.description: Use an “else if” statement in JavaScript.

badges.title: Until the End of Time
badges.description: Use a forever loop in JavaScript.

badges.title: Hey I’m Walking Here
badges.description: Use the overlapsWith function to see if two sprites are overlapping.

badges.title: Gaming the System
badges.description: Use the setGameOverEffect and gameOver functions to customize game over screens.

badges.title: The Final Countdown
badges.description: Use the info.onCountdownEnd function to run code when the countdown reaches zero.

badges.title: Playing the Odds
badges.description: Use the Math.percentChance function inside an if statement to add randomness to a project.

badges.title: A Flair for the Dramatic
badges.description: Add a custom sprite effect to a sprite.

badges.title: Let’s Try That Again
badges.description: Use the game.reset function to restart a project.
